note: Arithmetic checks out: 18%x0.95=17.1% plus 82%x0.04=3.28% gives 20.4% escalation; 1+0.5+0.204x10=3.54; unflagged errors 18%x0.05=0.9%.

Arithmetic defect in the premise: at n=300 and p=0.18 the binomial SD is 0.022, so a 0.25 boundary sits ~3.1 SD out and would fire well under once a year, not twice a week. Twice-weekly firing implies a denominator of roughly 10 per day. The stem's 300 requests/day and the stated alert frequency are not mutually consistent; C is still the right fix.

B is genuinely defensible and may be the key: normalising out the correlation id is entirely within the platform team's control and removes 38% of calls immediately, whereas A depends on another team funding work. I chose A because the redundant polling is a defect in the caller and the stem foregrounds ownership ('third-largest line', 'nobody owns that integration'), and because caching answers about a case that is still evolving reintroduces the staleness failure of ETO-C-045. To separate them the stem would need to say either that the source data is static while the case is open (favours B) or that the owning team is reachable/has budget (favours A).
Arithmetic consistent: 4.1x1.0 = 4.1 vs 1.3x3.2 = 4.16, i.e. flat per completed clearance.

B is defensible as the next step: sampling the rejections against labelled criteria distinguishes a bad gate from a bad generator directly. I chose C because an overnight step change in a measured rate should send you to the instrument's change log first, and C is minutes of work against hours for B. If the stem said the gate is under change control with no recent revision, C would collapse and B would be the clear answer.
Arithmetic consistent: 1.8s commitment less 1.55s current leaves 250ms headroom against a 400ms addition, so the interactive path cannot absorb it.

A is partially defensible - nothing waits on a score and the trend is read daily, so the batch path is a legitimate move - but it only halves a cost that D cuts by ~95%, and it does not address the actual error, which is that a trend needs a stable sample rather than complete coverage. Best done alongside D, not instead of it.

Minor: B only catches the failure if the parts master marks superseded status, since a superseded part number is still a real entry in the master. C is the cleaner catch. Both are still the only two measurement-of-correctness options.

Figures verified: model spend 12,000 -> 5,000 (-7,000); escalations 40,000 -> 48,000 at $6 = 240,000 -> 288,000 (+48,000); total 252,000 -> 293,000 (+41,000). Both A and D follow and no third option does. E is correctly false: break-even needs the resolution rate held within ~1.17 points, not three.

B and D overlap somewhat - both turn on exposure changing the denominator - but they are distinct claims (comparability across the boundary vs the raw count mechanism), so the pair is not a duplicate key.
